explanations.explanation: It’s the “end‐of‐sentence” signal—a feature that fires when a period (or similar terminal punctuation) marks a sentence’s boundary, so that the model subsequently shifts to a sentence–start prediction (e.g. choosing a capitalized or otherwise proper next token) instead of a continuation token.

This feature activates when the model is processing a possessive or ownership construction—whether via contracted possessives (like ’s) or language‐specific case markers—indicating that the token is part of a structure linking an entity to its attribute or possession.

It appears the model has learned a sub‐word “affix” signal—a feature that activates on certain word‐ending fragments that are morphologically or orthographically paired with a particular continuation. In effect, when that “suffix unit” is present (e.g. parts like “‐ur”, “‐in”, “‐ber”, “‐ash”, “‐led”, etc.), the model is biased toward one set of completions, whereas in its absence (the contrapositive), it predicts an alternate ending (often “‐ion,” “‐ley,” etc.). This suggests the feature is detecting and marking a latent morphemic pattern used in forming derived or inflected variants, guiding the model’s token‐prediction toward a consistent word‐ending transformation.

It’s a signal that fires at sentence‐ or clause–ending punctuation in structured, formal text—marking a boundary where the context resets (for example, at the final period of a citation or spec list) and influencing the model’s choice of the following token.

It’s a detector for a sentence‐ or segment–boundary marker—most notably the period—that signals a structured, formal break (as in announcements, lists, or numeric/date info) and that conditions the model’s next-token choices at these hard stops.

It’s a control signal for handling contraction‐ or possessive–apostrophe morphology—in other words, a feature that “notices” an apostrophe in the input and primes the network to produce the expected contraction ending (like “’s” or “’t”) in context.

The feature appears to encode a notion of “readiness or availability” in commercial or informational contexts—signaling that a product, service, or option is currently ready to be obtained or accessed.

It is a feature that “lights up” on clitic‐suffixes—especially the contracted or possessive ’s (and related forms like ’t)—marking when a word (often a proper name) is immediately modified by a contraction or possessive ending.

It detects when text is presenting a clock‐time (or time stamp) expression—that is, a numeral (especially “1”) immediately followed by a colon and a two‐digit minute value—and so marks the pattern used in dates, schedules, or posted timestamps.

This feature detects the contracted clitic “’s” (the apostrophe‐s marker), signaling a possessive or contraction (e.g. “he’s” as “he is/has”) and thereby marking a specific syntactic/grammatical construction.

In contexts like ads, news bulletins, or official notices, it boosts the probability of a terminal punctuation (typically a period) at the end of a self-contained segment—effectively indicating that the current formal text “block” is complete, whereas without it a different kind of continuation (often a numeral, letter, or other token) would be produced.

It detects and signals a “not only … but also …” contrastive or additive construction, activating when a sentence sets up one clause with “not only” so that a complementary, contrasting clause (“but also …”) follows.

explanations.explanation: It appears that the feature is detecting a sentence‐ or clause–boundary marker in formally structured, often technical or enumerative text. In other words, it “fires” strongly at punctuation (typically a period) that ends a structured or official statement, thereby signaling the segmentation of a statement before a transition to the next independent unit.

It’s a boundary‐signal feature—one that fires strongly at a sentence– or segment–end marker (often a period in structured or formal text) that cues a switch in formatting or token choice (for example, guiding the proper numerical/date or title continuation) in the next token.

It detects when a sentence or formal “data‐segment” is ending—namely, the full stop (or its equivalent in structured, often official or numeric text) that signals a boundary between discrete, formal information chunks.

It’s a “date‐format cue” feature—it fires when the context signals that a month abbreviation or date header has ended with punctuation so that the next token is treated as the numeric day (or other date‐piece) rather than a non–date word. In short, it encodes the formatting and context of dates to steer the model to output a proper day/token following a month or similar announcement.

It appears that this feature is firing in contexts where the model signals a conversational, evaluative tone—especially when expressing personal preferences or judgments (using words like “like” and informal contractions such as “don’t”). In other words, the feature captures a colloquial, opinion‐expressing register that guides the model toward phrasing typical of informal, subjective commentary.

It appears this feature is a kind of “boundary‐oriented” signal that fires when the model should insert a strong sentence or segment delimiter (typically a period) in formal or structured text. In doing so, it conditions the following token to fit contexts like dates, numbers, addresses, or other structured sequences—essentially controlling how the text is segmented and how the following token is chosen.
This feature appears to detect contraction sequences—in other words, it marks when an apostrophe is used to form a contracted auxiliary or pronoun (e.g. “’re”, “’s”, “’ve”, “’m”) in English.

It’s a “metadata header” indicator—that is, a feature that signals the model is in the blog‐entry header context (with date/time, “am/PM” markers, filing information, etc.) and so biases the next token toward the structured, meta-information style typical of post headers.

It appears that the feature is essentially a “sentence‐boundary” or “end‐of-thought” detector. In contexts where a final punctuation token (mostly periods) is used to terminate an independent clause or sentence, the feature is strongly activated. Its presence signals that the model is about to start a new sentence (or segment), thereby biasing the next token distribution toward sentence‐initial tokens, whereas without it the model would continue in a different style or context.

It appears this feature is detecting a punctuation‐boundary signal—in particular, the kind of sentence‐ or citation‐terminating period that appears in formal or structured text (legal notices, technical descriptions, product listings, etc.). In doing so it strongly conditions what token comes next (often an uppercase or title‐styled token), and when the feature’s effect is removed the model’s next-token prediction shifts accordingly.

It marks text that isn’t “content” per se but boilerplate metadata—the structured, formulaic strings (timestamps, uploader or source credits, URLs/components like “IP,” “amp,” “from,” “at,” etc.) that appear in online pages and posts.

It appears this feature acts as a boundary‐signal marker that “bookends” formal, structured information—such as dates, event announcements, addresses, and numeric details—so that when a sentence or section ends (often signaled by a period), it properly conditions the start of a new context (e.g. adjusting capitalization, spacing, or numeral/formatted token choices).

It appears that this feature is signaling a “contraposition” or inversion marker in the text—a kind of internal flag that, when active, cues the model to switch from the immediately surface-level input (usually a question, prompt, or “call‐to‐action” phrase) to generating a contrasting or reformulated (often answer‐like or clarifying) continuation. In short, it represents an abstract contrapositive or reversal signal in the model’s internal representation of discourse.
It appears this feature lights up strongly on tokens that serve as sentence‐ or clause–final punctuation (especially periods) marking a completed, self–contained statement.

It appears that this feature “lights up” at the boundaries of formally structured segments—that is, it recognizes markers (often punctuation like periods) that signal the end of a title, announcement, or official statement. In short, it detects sentence‐ or clause‐final boundaries in formal or structured text.

This feature appears to detect and signal sentence‐ or clause–terminating punctuation (typically a period), which then resets context so that the next token is chosen in a distinct “new sentence” or formatting role (often a number, capital letter, or special token).

It’s a high‐level “example/hypothetical setup” detector—that is, the feature fires in contexts where an illustrative or conditional scenario is being introduced (as in “For example” or “For instance…”) so that the model expects to continue with a clause (often with “if”) rather than a noun phrase.

It appears this feature encodes a kind of conditional‐or “if–then–but not” signal—a latent indicator that a statement is being presented in a context of rules or exceptions such that the following token is “flipped” to its contrapositive (or alternate) form.

It appears that this feature is “noticing” a particular subword – often an affix‐ or contraction-like fragment that marks a boundary between parts of a word or phrase. When the feature is active, the model tends to complete or punctuate the compound differently than it would if that subword marker were absent. In short, the feature signals a fine‐grained morphological/orthographic segmentation (or clitic boundary) that in turn alters which token (or ending) is generated next.

It appears that this feature “lights up” whenever the context is setting up a planned, conditional, or normative continuation—that is, when the sentence shifts into an anticipatory or decision‐making clause. In other words, the feature signals that the upcoming phrase will express an intention, expectation, or evaluative turn (as seen by the high activations on words like “those,” “to,” “how,” “should,” “would,” etc.), and it biases the model toward selecting function words that mark that transition in discourse.

It’s a feature that “lights up” when a token is the final fragment of a proper‐noun or title string—for example, the ending syllable of a company name, place name, person’s name, or formal initiative—and thus signals that the model is in a context of named entities or titles.

It seems the feature is responsible for steering which closed‐class word (such as an article, determiner, or possessive marker) is produced next—in effect, it encodes contextual “decisions” about definiteness, possession, and style for noun phrases.

This feature is sensitive to formal, announcement‐ or headline–style segments that list structured event details (e.g. dates, locations, awards, scheduled activities) and terminate with a clearly demarcated sentence boundary (typically a period).

It appears that this feature activates on tokens that serve as the “start‐pieces” of multi–token words—often proper names, brands, or technical terms. In other words, it detects when a subword is functioning as the initial fragment of a larger lexical unit, strongly signaling a specific continuation.

It appears this feature is picking up on when the context calls for “introducing” a new referent—that is, a syntactic‐semantic signal favoring the start of an indefinite (or otherwise new) noun phrase (marked by “a” or similar) over a pronominal or referential alternative (like “it,” “him,” etc.). In other words, the feature activates in contexts—often in headline, announcement, or imperative styles—where the model is about to “launch” a new entity description.

It’s a feature that “lights up” on subword endings—that is, it recognizes when a word has been split into its base and a final suffix or affix fragment (often seen in technical terms, names, or adjectives), signaling the morphologically or stylistically modified tail‐part of a compound token.
